# STAT 110 (synthetic) — Lecture notes

## §1 Conditional probability

§1.1 P(A | B) is read "the probability of A among B". It answers: of the
cases in group B, what share are also in A?

§1.2 Compute it as (number of cases in both A and B) divided by (number of
cases in B). The denominator is the reference group B, not the whole sample.

§1.3 The order matters. P(A | B) and P(B | A) usually differ because they use
different reference groups. Before computing, decide which group the question
restricts you to; that group is the denominator.

§1.4 Assume every case is equally weighted and the reference group is not
empty.

## §2 Two-way tables

§2.1 A two-way table counts cases by two categorical variables at once, one in
the rows and one in the columns, with row totals and column totals.

§2.2 A row percentage divides a cell by its row total; a column percentage
divides a cell by its column total. Choosing row versus column percentages is
the same decision as choosing the reference group in §1.2.

§2.3 Row percentages in one row add to 100%; column percentages in one column
add to 100%. Percentages across a row of column percentages need not.

## §3 Grouped summaries

§3.1 A grouped summary splits the cases by a categorical variable and computes
one summary value (such as a mean or a count) per group.

§3.2 The result has one row per non-empty group, not one row per original case.

§3.3 Compare groups using the same summary; do not compare a group mean with a
group total.

Progress is saved in batches, so recent changes may remain only in this chat until saved.



Conditional probability asks: **within a particular group, what share also meets another condition?** Your notes read \(P(A\mid B)\) as “the probability of A among B.” The group after the bar—\(B\)—is your **reference group**. ([Notes §1.1–1.2](materials/notes.md))

For equally weighted cases and a nonempty reference group:

\[
P(A\mid B)=
\frac{\text{number of cases in both A and B}}
{\text{number of cases in B}}.
\]

For a new example using that rule, imagine 100 students:

- 40 are commuters.
- 16 of those commuters bike to campus.
- 20 students in total bike to campus.

What is the probability that a student bikes **given that they commute**?

“Given that they commute” restricts us to the **40 commuters**. Of those, 16 bike:

\[
P(\text{bikes}\mid\text{commutes})
=\frac{16}{40}
=\boxed{\text{40.0\% of commuters}}.
\]

The denominator is 40 because we’re asking about commuters. The other students fall outside the reference group.

**Reversing the condition changes the question.** If we ask what share commute **among students who bike**, the reference group becomes the 20 students who bike:

\[
P(\text{commutes}\mid\text{bikes})
=\frac{16}{20}
=\boxed{\text{80.0\% of students who bike}}.
\]

The overlap stays at 16, but the denominator changes. That is why \(P(A\mid B)\) and \(P(B\mid A)\) usually differ. ([Notes §1.3](materials/notes.md))

Your exam cue: **name the reference group first, then count the target cases inside it.** Report the answer as a percentage to one decimal place and name that group, as your [outline requires](materials/outline.md).

Try one: Of 30 students who work part-time, 12 commute. What is \(P(\text{commutes}\mid\text{works part-time})\)? Include the reference group in your answer.
